title: The Gang Carries a Corpse Up a Mountain

jokes.text: Frank criticizes using stew as a 'reviving mechanism' vs. food
jokes.setup: Someone (Dennis) has apparently been using stew as a reviving mechanism rather than food
jokes.punchline: 'cause you're using it as food, instead of using it as a reviving mechanism
jokes.explanation: Cold open absurdist detail — the idea that someone would use stew as a 'reviving mechanism' is a funny throwaway that establishes the gang's bizarre logic. Good economy, mild laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You got piss in that canteen?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: No, I got Gatorade in that canteen. The other one's got the piss in case things go bad.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Oh, goddamn it. Are you telling me there's gonna be obnoxious Americans on this hike? 'Cause that's the last thing I want to see.' — delivered while he himself is an obnoxious American in Ireland
jokes.setup: Dennis spots a truck of fellow Americans while hiking in Ireland
jokes.punchline: He complains about obnoxious Americans with zero self-awareness that he is exactly that
jokes.explanation: Classic Dennis narcissism/lack of self-awareness. The irony is tight and character-specific — Dennis genuinely believes he is different from other Americans. Works because it foreshadows the entire episode's theme.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I see you all fell for my ruse.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: What ruse?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You asking us to go on a hike with your dad, and us saying yes? Oldest trick in the book.

jokes.text: 'You got piss in that canteen?' / 'No, I got Gatorade in that canteen.' [beat] 'The other one's got the piss in case things go bad.'
jokes.setup: Mac suspects the canteen has piss; Frank reassures him it's Gatorade
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately reveals the OTHER canteen has piss — he has a designated piss canteen as a contingency
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is nearly perfect: Mac's suspicion is subverted (no, it's Gatorade), then immediately one-upped (but there IS a piss canteen). The beat between lines is key. 'In case things go bad' is the perfect Frank rationalization — he has a contingency piss supply. Pure character comedy, highly quotable, and it pays off devastatingly at [15:01]. Earns its high score through economy, surprise, and character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You know, no offense, Charlie, but Shelley's fat as shit.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, no offense taken, Dennis, because he is fat as shit, but, um, he won't really mind us saying that because he's dead.

jokes.text: Charlie reveals his 'ruse': he tricked the gang into agreeing to a hike with his dad
jokes.setup: Charlie announces 'I see you all fell for my ruse'
jokes.punchline: The 'ruse' was just... asking them to do something, and them saying yes
jokes.explanation: Charlie's delusional self-satisfaction at a 'ruse' that is literally just normal human social interaction is perfect Charlie logic. The back-and-forth with Dennis ('Asking someone to do something?' / 'Exactly.' / 'And then, them doing it?' / 'Precisely, yes.') is well-structured escalating absurdism. Very Charlie-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: What? What the hell are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I'm talking about Shelley Kelly, my dad. He's dead.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh. Shit.

jokes.text: 'You know, no offense, Charlie, but Shelley's fat as shit.' / 'Oh, no offense taken, Dennis, because he is fat as shit, but...he won't really mind us saying that because he's dead.'
jokes.setup: Dennis insults Shelley's weight; Charlie graciously accepts the remark
jokes.punchline: Charlie reveals Shelley doesn't mind because he's dead — the reveal that the whole premise is about a corpse
jokes.explanation: The episode's central premise reveal. The structure is excellent: the fat joke serves as the vehicle for the death reveal, making the punchline doubly surprising. Charlie's matter-of-fact delivery ('he won't really mind us saying that because he's dead') is pitch-perfect dark comedy. The setup earns the punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: All right? Look, it's a Kelly family burial tradition. We're just gonna carry the man to the top of the mountain, and then we're gonna chuck him over the side.

jokes.text: Beat after Charlie announces 'He's dead' — the group's silent stunned reaction before 'Oh. Shit.'
jokes.setup: Charlie announces his dad is dead and they're supposed to carry the body up a mountain
jokes.punchline: Long pause followed by a simple, deflated 'Oh. Shit.' from someone in the group
jokes.explanation: The silence-then-deflated-reaction is a reliable comedy beat. 'Oh. Shit.' is good in its simplicity but it's a fairly standard reaction beat — functional, not inspired.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, why would I want to ruin my essence, Mac? I'm not doing it.

jokes.text: Dennis refuses to carry the body citing back concerns, then immediately has to backpedal when Mac calls out his claim that his back has 'the symmetry of the Vitruvian man'
jokes.setup: Dennis claims he can't carry the body because of his back; Mac quotes Dennis's own previous boast about his back being Vitruvian-man perfect
jokes.punchline: 'Yeah, well, why would I want to ruin my essence, Mac? I'm not doing it.'
jokes.explanation: Deep Dennis character comedy — his narcissism about his own physique is a running character trait and Mac's ability to quote him verbatim is funny. 'The symmetry of the Vitruvian man' as a self-description is very Dennis. His pivot to 'why would I want to ruin my essence?' works perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: So I'm just gonna blurt it right out. Bros before hoes.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Uh, he's right. Bros before hoes.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah, he's got us. Oh, my God. Yeah.

jokes.text: Charlie declares an emergency and invokes 'Bros before hoes' as a catch-all persuasion tool to get the gang to carry a corpse
jokes.setup: Charlie needs to convince the gang to carry his dead dad up a mountain
jokes.punchline: His persuasive trump card is 'Bros before hoes' which the guys immediately accept as ironclad logic, while Dee correctly points out it makes no sense
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of treating 'Bros before hoes' as a universal logical override — and all the men immediately submitting to it — is very true to these characters. Dee's protest ('That doesn't fit here. Bros before hoes? What does that have to do with anything?') and the response 'That's sort of a catch-all, Dee' is the best line in the exchange. Well-earned gang-logic comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: That doesn't fit here. Bros before hoes? What does that have to do with anything?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: That's sort of a catch-all, Dee.

jokes.text: 'And hoes, too.' — Frank adding Dee into the 'Bros before hoes' chant
jokes.setup: The gang chants 'Bros before hoes' while Dee is standing right there
jokes.punchline: Frank tacks on 'And hoes, too' as an afterthought, ostensibly being inclusive but actually just emphasizing the insult
jokes.explanation: Quick, economical punchline tag on the Bros before hoes bit. Frank adding 'and hoes, too' reads as performative generosity while still calling Dee a hoe. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: What if we burn the body and carry the ashes up the hill? No, no. I could consecrate them.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Look, no one is going to torch or consummate all over my dad.

jokes.text: Dennis suggests burning the body and carrying ashes, then quickly clarifies 'I could consecrate them'
jokes.setup: Dennis proposes a practical solution to the heavy body problem
jokes.punchline: He adds 'I could consecrate them' as if religious ceremony is what makes the difference between acceptable and unacceptable body disposal
jokes.explanation: Minor joke. Dennis's self-appointed authority to 'consecrate' things is a small character beat. Functional but not memorable.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Bros before hoes, Dee. Frank, can I please have a white wine spritzer?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: No, no, they're for Charlie.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Charlie... Charlie, order me a wine spritzer, please.

jokes.text: 'Look, no one is going to torch or consummate all over my dad.'
jokes.setup: Dennis suggests burning the body and consecrating the ashes
jokes.punchline: Charlie mishears/misuses 'consecrate' as 'consummate' — implying a very different act
jokes.explanation: Charlie's malapropism game is one of the show's most reliable devices, and 'consummate' for 'consecrate' is a great one — the accidental implication is hilariously inappropriate given the context (his dead dad). Pure Charlie, highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: What if we chop the body up? Come on. And we carry it in pieces, right? Or-or melt it somehow.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Like you did to Dee's doctor guy?

jokes.text: Frank immediately offers Charlie snacks and wine spritzers while they're supposed to be carrying the body
jokes.setup: In the middle of carrying a corpse up a hill, Frank interrupts to offer egg, GORP, or a wine spritzer
jokes.punchline: The juxtaposition of mundane hospitality against the absurd situation, plus the specificity of 'GORP' and 'wine spritzer'
jokes.explanation: Establishes the spritzer running gag and Frank's butler role. 'GORP' is a funny specific word choice. Functional setup for bigger spritzer jokes later.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Well, well, that doctor showed up at the castle, and you weren't there, so Dennis poured hot oil on him.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: What?!

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Shut up! Come on!

jokes.text: Mac demands a wine spritzer via Charlie because of 'Bros before hoes'; the spritzer ordering chain through Charlie
jokes.setup: Frank will only serve Charlie due to the Bros before hoes rule; everyone must order through Charlie
jokes.punchline: This creates an absurd ordering protocol where grown adults must route drink orders through Charlie like a medieval lord
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the Bros before hoes absurdity into a practical logistical problem. The escalation of Dennis not wanting a spritzer but being spritzed anyway adds to the comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: It-it wasn't even that hot.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Did you use the murder hole?

jokes.text: Frank accidentally reveals Dennis poured hot oil on Dee's doctor at the castle
jokes.setup: Dennis suggests 'melt it somehow, like you did to Dee's doctor guy'
jokes.punchline: Frank casually confirms Dennis poured hot oil on a doctor Dee had a romantic interest in — a secret nobody told Dee
jokes.explanation: Classic Sunny revelation structure — a horrifying fact dropped casually mid-task. Dennis scalding a potential suitor for Dee with a medieval murder hole is perfectly in character. The escalation 'Did you use the murder hole?' from someone in the group normalizes it further. The timing mid-corpse-carry makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You weren't there to enjoy him so I enjoyed him, per the castle's wishes.

jokes.text: Dennis suggests chopping the body up or melting it, Frank reveals Dennis previously poured hot oil on Dee's doctor
jokes.setup: Dennis matter-of-factly suggests chopping or melting Shelley's body as a practical solution
jokes.punchline: Frank reveals Dennis already has experience with this: 'Did you melt it, like you did to Dee's doctor guy?'
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark comedy — the reveal that Dennis casually scalded a doctor with hot oil as a previous side adventure is played completely matter-of-factly. The rewatch bonus comes from the callousness. 'Dee's doctor guy' is perfect casual Dennis dismissiveness.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You-you killed my dad with your stupid banshee curse.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: My stupid what?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: That's why he died. Every Kelly saw a banshee right before he died. My dad saw you, so, you got to be here.

jokes.text: 'You weren't there to enjoy him so I enjoyed him, per the castle's wishes.'
jokes.setup: Dee is furious Dennis scalded her doctor; Dennis explains his justification
jokes.punchline: 'You weren't there to enjoy him so I enjoyed him, per the castle's wishes' — Dennis treating a person as an experience to be 'enjoyed' and deferring to a castle's wishes
jokes.explanation: Two jokes in one line. First: Dennis treating Dee's doctor as an 'experience' to be 'enjoyed' (I.e., he scalded him FOR FUN) is perfectly sociopathic Dennis. Second: 'per the castle's wishes' is a magnificent absurdist detail — Dennis is taking orders from a castle. This is exceptional character comedy that could ONLY come from Dennis and only in this show's universe. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: We don't even need you. We were probably gonna throw you from the top anyway!

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I thought about it.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Did you think about?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I did, too.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: God.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I was thinking about it, too, yeah.

jokes.text: 'Are you still talking to the castle?! I thought that was a COVID thing!'
jokes.setup: Dennis says he acted 'per the castle's wishes'
jokes.punchline: Dee's outraged response implies this was an ongoing thing — and she thought the castle-talking was a COVID-era aberration, not a permanent personality trait
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation off #16. The fact that there's a whole context where Dennis talked to a castle during COVID — and Dee had optimistically assumed it was a temporary crisis behavior — is brilliantly absurd. The COVID justification makes it feel very real and of-its-time. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Well, it's that monstrous spine of hers, you know? The scoliosis hardened it into petrified wood, unlike my back which is pretty much all muscle.

jokes.text: Charlie guilts Dee into staying by claiming she caused his dad's death with her 'banshee curse'
jokes.setup: Dee tries to leave the corpse-carrying expedition
jokes.punchline: Charlie insists she has to stay because as a banshee, she cursed and killed his dad — Dee screeching = banshee mythology applied literally
jokes.explanation: Calling Dee a banshee is a great character-specific insult — it's both an attack on her screeching voice/personality AND a piece of Irish folklore that Charlie takes completely literally. 'Every Kelly saw a banshee right before he died' is excellent mythology-building for Charlie's delusional worldview.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Were you not carrying it? Not carr... What are you talking about, man? Not carrying it?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah, I was carrying it.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Why did it get lighter?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, my God.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: It looks like he was dragging his feet back here.

jokes.text: Dee gets hit or hurt by something immediately after saying 'Charlie, banshees aren't real!' — the group asks 'Is that it? Is that what it was?'
jokes.setup: Dee insists banshees aren't real right after Charlie invokes the banshee curse
jokes.punchline: Something immediately injures or startles Dee, and everyone takes this as confirmation of the banshee curse
jokes.explanation: Classic Dee-gets-hurt physical comedy. The timing — immediately after denying the curse — is good structure. 'Is that it? Is that what it was?' is well-delivered escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah, I was hanging on the bag a little bit. You know, just from moment to moment, you know, just a tiny, tiny bit, okay? I was trying to decompress my Vitruvian spine. I'm sorry!

jokes.text: The gang casually discusses possibly throwing Dee off the top of the mountain 'to play it safe' in case she's a witch
jokes.setup: Dee threatens to leave; the gang considers whether she might be a banshee or witch
jokes.punchline: 'We were probably gonna throw you from the top anyway' / 'I thought about it' / 'Did you think about it?' / 'I did, too' / 'You got to play it safe, you know?' / 'What if she's a witch?'
jokes.explanation: The casual, overlapping way the gang discusses possibly murdering Dee is perfect dark comedy — no one is really alarmed, it's just a reasonable precaution they'd all apparently been considering. 'What if she's a witch?' as a repeated kicker is a good tag.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Now as a Dutch man, I think I would look at this the way I would think of a windmill or a dam. Cool. How's a windmill gonna help us? I haven't been Dutch long enough to know.

jokes.text: Dennis notes 'I hate to admit it, but this is a lot heavier without Dee. It's that monstrous spine of hers — the scoliosis hardened it into petrified wood'
jokes.setup: Without Dee, they're struggling with the body bag
jokes.punchline: Dennis attributes Dee's carrying power to her scoliosis having 'hardened [her spine] into petrified wood' — a grotesque body-horror insult delivered as a neutral observation
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Dennis insult. 'The scoliosis hardened it into petrified wood' is inventive, specific, and grotesque in the most satisfying way — it's not just 'Dee has a bad back,' it's that her deformity has become a structural asset. Dennis delivers it as a compliment, which makes it worse. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Oh. Oh. Okay, that's my bad. Oh. Okay. That is, uh... That's gonna be a mess inside that bag, guys. Oh, yeah. That's one big sack of Irish stew.

jokes.text: It's revealed Dennis was not carrying the body but riding/hanging on it — the body felt LIGHTER when he 'let go'
jokes.setup: Dennis claims to have tripped, but Mac and Frank notice the bag got lighter when Dennis left
jokes.punchline: Dennis was hanging ON the body bag, not carrying it — he was taking a ride on his friend's dead father
jokes.explanation: Superb physical gag revealed through dialogue logic. The clue — 'the body got lighter' — leads perfectly to the revelation. Dennis riding a corpse to 'decompress his Vitruvian spine' is peak Dennis narcissism. His defensive justification ('just from moment to moment, you know, just a tiny, tiny bit') is excellent character voice.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You guys are gonna want to hear this. So, uh, uh, Dutch first. Dutch first, then gay, then problem solver. Now could you repeat that back to me?

jokes.text: 'I told you guys it was something I was worried about... I was trying to decompress my Vitruvian spine. I'm sorry!'
jokes.setup: Dennis is caught having ridden the corpse instead of carrying it
jokes.punchline: He justifies it by referencing his earlier stated concern about his Vitruvian back, as if this was a reasonable medical accommodation
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the Vitruvian man back bit. 'Decompress my Vitruvian spine' by riding a dead man is insane Dennis logic delivered with earnest self-justification. Character-specific and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: All right, you're Irish, Mac. Yeah. You're not Dutch.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: What? You're Irish.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Right, but we knew you were gonna be so goddamn annoying about it on the trip, and that it was gonna be the only thing you talked about, so we paid your mom to tell you you were Dutch.

jokes.text: Mac declares he will approach the steep hill 'as a Dutch man' and 'think of it like a windmill or a dam'
jokes.setup: Mac has recently discovered/been told he is Dutch and is trying on the identity
jokes.punchline: Mac's application of 'Dutch thinking' is to suggest a windmill or dam, which are his entire mental model of Dutchness
jokes.explanation: Mac's Dutch identity crisis is a strong running gag for the episode. The reduction of Dutch culture to 'windmill or dam' is a good joke about surface-level national stereotyping. Sets up the killer punchline perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: It cost us a couple of loosies.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah, your mom does not like you, dude.

jokes.text: 'Cool. How's a windmill gonna help us?' / 'I haven't been Dutch long enough to know.'
jokes.setup: Mac invokes Dutch windmill thinking as a solution to carrying a corpse uphill
jokes.punchline: 'I haven't been Dutch long enough to know' — Mac's Dutch identity is so new he hasn't had time to develop actual Dutch engineering knowledge
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'I haven't been Dutch long enough to know' is perfectly constructed — it accepts the absurd premise (you can BE Dutch and have Dutch knowledge) while also being a completely reasonable-sounding statement. The delivery of this as a sincere explanation is what elevates it. Exceptional economy and originality.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I'm gonna get another shamrock tattoo on the other leg!

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Don't you dare!

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm gonna do it!

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Don't you dare get another shamrock tattoo, you son of a bitch!

jokes.text: Mac then suggests 'If we had a really giant windmill, we could just blow him up the hill' — everyone momentarily agrees
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to apply Dutch windmill thinking
jokes.punchline: The 'solution' is a giant windmill to blow the corpse up — and the others riff on it positively for a moment before reality kicks in
jokes.explanation: Decent absurdist follow-through on the windmill idea. The beat where they all briefly consider 'giant windmill' as viable is funny but doesn't quite reach the heights of the setup joke.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You know, he slaved away as a cheese monster, or whatever. He died with his lungs filled with fluid, he was gasping for air.

jokes.text: Dennis claims the tent-sliding was 'actually a back-strengthening exercise' for him
jokes.setup: Everyone is noting the successful tent slide
jokes.punchline: Dennis reframes the activity as beneficial for his precious back, completely reversing his earlier concern
jokes.explanation: Minor callback. Dennis's ability to reframe any situation to reflect well on him is good character work, but this is a small beat compared to others.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: COVID?! But so-so the poor guy's dying from a banshee curse, and now he's got to deal with COVID on top of everything else?

jokes.text: 'That's one big sack of Irish stew.' — referring to the body bag after it's been knocked around
jokes.setup: The body bag has been rolling, dropped, slid — it's been mangled
jokes.punchline: Mac's clinical description of the liquefied remains as 'one big sack of Irish stew' — also callbacks the opening stew line
jokes.explanation: Sharp dark comedy with beautiful economy. 'One big sack of Irish stew' is both a callback to the opening stew and a grotesquely accurate description of what happens to a body after this treatment. Highly quotable. The callousness is pitch-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: What, do you think I'm shooting COVID laser beams out of my eyeballs?

jokes.text: Dennis's solution: dump out 'whatever liquid is probably in that body bag' to lighten the load
jokes.setup: The body bag has been mangled; they need to lighten it
jokes.punchline: Dennis's practical engineering solution is to drain the body fluids — presented as a completely normal logistical suggestion
jokes.explanation: Dennis's cold practicality about draining a body bag is characteristically Dennis. Good dark comedy, presented as normal problem-solving.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Of course there is! The-the-the hydro pills and the... and the bleach, and the... the horse dewormer. The-the president's stuff!

jokes.text: Dennis announces 'I'm starting to see myself as more of a problem solver' and declares it a 'new identity' to put on the list: 'Dutch first, then gay, then problem solver'
jokes.setup: Dennis suggests draining body fluids as a solution and feels good about it
jokes.punchline: He declares 'problem solver' a new identity to add to a list of his identities — and Mac already has a priority-ordered identity list: 'Dutch first, then gay, then problem solver'
jokes.explanation: Mac's identity crisis given a crisp, ordered list is excellent character comedy. 'Dutch first, then gay, then problem solver' is a perfect encapsulation of Mac's season-long arc of self-discovery presented as an absurd hierarchy. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Where they put the thing in your arm with the chip, and it goes inside your body? I heard the nerd on the island talk about them. That once they get that thing inside of you, they can control your thoughts. They take your thoughts, download 'em, put 'em into a manatee.

jokes.text: The gang reveals they paid Mac's mom with 'a couple of loosies' to tell Mac he was Dutch — it was a lie to get him to stop talking about his identity
jokes.setup: Mac is leaning into his Dutch identity; it's revealed this was all a ruse
jokes.punchline: They paid Mac's famously terrible mother with cigarettes ('loosies') to lie to her son about his heritage — and his mom accepted
jokes.explanation: Multi-layered dark joke: (1) the gang was so annoyed by Mac's identity talking they fabricated a nationality, (2) Mac's mom sold out her son for cigarettes, (3) it backfired because now Mac talks about identity EVEN MORE. 'It cost us a couple of loosies' and 'your mom does not like you, dude' are both great lines.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: been ruined by tiny cars, castle beds and... Goddamn. I hate this godforsaken country!

jokes.text: 'Yeah, but, I mean, Luther Vandross? Mac, really?' — referring to whatever Dutch ancestor name they invented for Mac
jokes.setup: The gang is confronting Mac about the Dutch lie
jokes.punchline: The fabricated Dutch ancestor's name was apparently 'Luther Vandross' — an absurd choice
jokes.explanation: The reveal that the gang chose 'Luther Vandross' as a Dutch ancestor name is a perfect absurd specific detail. It raises questions (why Luther Vandross?) that make it funnier. Good character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: For what it's worth, I'm sorry I'm not your real dad.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Thanks, Frank. I'm kind of sorry, too.

jokes.text: Mac threatens to get ANOTHER shamrock tattoo on the other leg in retaliation — 'I'm gonna do it!' / 'Don't you dare!'
jokes.setup: The gang wants Mac to get rid of his shamrock tattoo; Mac is furious about the Dutch lie
jokes.punchline: Mac's retaliation threat is to double down on the worst tattoo possible — getting a matching shamrock on the other leg
jokes.explanation: Mac's spite-tattoo threat is a perfect character beat — his stubbornness expressed through self-harm. 'Don't you dare get another shamrock tattoo, you son of a bitch!' from Dennis is a great reaction. The stakes of the argument being a shamrock tattoo is delightfully petty.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Aah! Whoa! Is that piss? Oh! That's not supposed to be the piss one! Why do you have a piss one?

jokes.text: After Mac leaves, the gang quietly admits 'he was carrying a ton of weight' — 'That would be another one of his annoying identities... The man who could carry stuff.'
jokes.setup: Mac stormed off; they're now struggling without him
jokes.punchline: They acknowledge his value but frame it as another 'annoying identity' he'd have — 'The man who could carry stuff'
jokes.explanation: Good callback. The gang's grudging respect for Mac expressed through their own self-serving framing ('annoying identity') is perfectly in character. The specificity of 'The man who could carry stuff' is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, give me that. Wash it out with Gatorade.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Goddamn it, Frank!

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Ooh.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Huh?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: That's piss, too!

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, no!

jokes.text: 'COVID?! But so-so the poor guy's dying from a banshee curse, and now he's got to deal with COVID on top of everything else?'
jokes.setup: Mac reveals the symptoms sound like COVID; Charlie is informed his dad may have had COVID
jokes.punchline: Charlie's response treats the banshee curse AND COVID as simultaneously real and separate afflictions that poor Shelley had to deal with simultaneously
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and among the best Charlie moments. The genius is that Charlie doesn't dismiss the banshee curse — he accepts COVID as an ADDITIONAL burden his dad had to suffer on top of the existing curse. His empathy for his dad dealing with 'two things at once' is heartbreaking and hilarious simultaneously. Pure Charlie logic, perfectly delivered, and deeply character-integrated. Near-perfect Charlie joke.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Oh, I must have got confused and pissed in 'em both. Wait, wait, wait. I got you a spritzer! How about a spritzer?

jokes.text: 'Did you give him COVID, Dennis?' / 'Me?! I never even interacted with the man. I was behind a stone wall and a painting that night.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is accused of giving Shelley COVID
jokes.punchline: Dennis's alibi is that he was 'behind a stone wall and a painting' — which explains his behavior but raises far more questions
jokes.explanation: 'I was behind a stone wall and a painting that night' is a brilliantly specific Dennis alibi that perfectly evokes the castle setting and his voyeuristic/predatory tendencies. It's a non-answer that answers nothing while revealing everything about Dennis's behavior.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, Dee, don't worry about it, because as soon as I figure out who or what I am, you'll never see me again!

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You're Irish.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You're Irish.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You are Irish!

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You are Irish!

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You're an Irishman!

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Shh!

jokes.text: 'What, do you think I'm shooting COVID laser beams out of my eyeballs?'
jokes.setup: Mac presses Dennis on how he could have spread COVID
jokes.punchline: Dennis's indignant counter-argument invokes 'COVID laser beams out of my eyeballs' as an absurd standard he's being held to
jokes.explanation: Good defensive absurdism from Dennis. 'COVID laser beams out of my eyeballs' is a funny specific choice for his straw man argument. Quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I will speak at whatever volume I choose, and if you don't like it, you can suck my big fat dick! One volume? For every single person in the whole wide world? That's socialism, and I won't stand for it!

jokes.text: Frank's 'vaccination' was 'hydro pills, bleach, horse dewormer — the president's stuff!'
jokes.setup: Frank claims to be 'fully vaccinated' despite not getting the shot
jokes.punchline: 'I got the non-shot kind' — hydro pills, bleach, horse dewormer, 'the president's stuff'
jokes.explanation: Frank's COVID misinformation beliefs are well-drawn character comedy. The specificity of 'the president's stuff' is a good, knowing reference without being preachy. Very Frank that he thinks he's fully vaccinated because he consumed these things.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: We are America, sweetheart! And we carry our country with us wherever we go! Because we love her! And when you love someone, you can't bear to leave 'em behind! Not ever!

jokes.text: Frank's anti-vax reasoning: 'Where they put the thing in your arm with the chip... they can control your thoughts. They take your thoughts, download 'em, put 'em into a manatee.'
jokes.setup: Frank explains why he didn't get the COVID vaccine
jokes.punchline: The conspiracy theory escalates to its logical conclusion: mind-control chips that download your thoughts into a manatee
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. Frank's conspiracy theory hits all the familiar beats (chips, mind control) but then takes a surreal turn to 'put 'em into a manatee' — which is both completely unexpected and somehow internally consistent with conspiracy logic (they're harvesting your thoughts for some aquatic mammal purpose). 'The nerd on the island' adds texture. The manatee is the perfect specific absurd detail. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: This isn't fair. I shouldn't have to carry you up this hill. You never carried me up a hill. You never picked me up from school. You didn't read me bedtime stories. You didn't carry me on your shoulders. You didn't bounce me on... You weren't there!

jokes.text: 'To be fair, COVID killed your dad. I just gave it to him.' — Frank apologizing while minimizing
jokes.setup: Frank is accused of killing Charlie's dad by giving him COVID
jokes.punchline: Frank's 'fair' distinction: COVID killed Shelley, Frank merely transmitted it — a legal/moral hairsplitting that is both technically true and completely monstrous
jokes.explanation: Perfect Frank line. The hair-splitting between 'gave someone a fatal disease' and 'killed them' is exactly the kind of monstrous-but-technically-valid logic Frank deploys. Economy is exceptional — maximum dark comedy per word. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Ah, Frank's right. I'm glad you're dead. I'm glad you're dead. Now I don't have to spend the rest of my life waiting for you to pick me up.

jokes.text: Dennis's back finally gives out at a dramatic moment — 'It's the end of the Vitruvian era! It's over! ...been ruined by tiny cars, castle beds and... I hate this godforsaken country!'
jokes.setup: Dennis has been protecting his precious back throughout; it finally gives out
jokes.punchline: Dennis declares 'the end of the Vitruvian era' as if his bad back is a civilizational collapse, listing the indignities that caused it: tiny cars, castle beds
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the Vitruvian back running gag. 'The end of the Vitruvian era' is an excellent turn of phrase — Dennis's narcissism extends to naming an era after his own physique. 'Tiny cars, castle beds' as the list of Ireland's crimes is characteristically Dennis. Good payoff to a well-built gag.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: It was supposed to go in the water. Maybe they usually do this at high tide. They probably did, yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah. Well, the birds will get him.

jokes.text: After Dennis collapses dramatically, someone says 'Hey, he's probably faking it.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has a dramatic back injury collapse
jokes.punchline: The response is immediate dismissal — 'He's probably faking it' — which given Dennis's history is completely reasonable
jokes.explanation: Quick, earned reaction beat. The gang's instinctive suspicion of Dennis is well-grounded in his history of manipulation and performance.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: But there's a bunch of kids down there.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, there's kids! Are there kids?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, shit. Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, that's good, then. They'll find the body. And they'll call the cops. It-It'll be sort of like a Stand by Me situation.

jokes.text: Frank apologizes to Charlie for giving his dad COVID, then adds 'I mean, if that's the case. I mean, we don't have proof. It's kind of like the Epstein thing.'
jokes.setup: Frank is apologizing for killing Charlie's dad
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately hedges his apology by comparing the evidence to the Epstein case — withdrawing moral responsibility while technically expressing remorse
jokes.explanation: Frank's conditional apology is well-executed. The Epstein comparison as a framework for plausible deniability is darkly funny. Very Frank.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You want to get some stew?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: God, no. That stew's gross.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, man. Stew?

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Oh, it is kind of nasty.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You guys want to go to McDonald's?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Oh, yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, McDonald's.
USA! USA! USA!

jokes.text: 'For what it's worth, I'm sorry I'm not your real dad.' [pause] 'Thanks, Frank. I'm kind of sorry, too.'
jokes.setup: Frank and Charlie share a quiet moment of emotional honesty
jokes.punchline: The exchange about Frank not being Charlie's real dad is delivered with perfect deadpan sadness — 'I'm kind of sorry, too' is both touching and funny
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most surprising moments — the genuine emotional beat lands because it's earned by context and because 'I'm kind of sorry, too' is pitch-perfect. It's simultaneously touching and funny, the best version of this show's dark-emotional comedy. The economy is exceptional.

jokes.text: Frank gives Charlie a canteen to drink from — Charlie immediately spits it out. 'Is that piss?' / 'Oh! That's not supposed to be the piss one!'
jokes.setup: Frank tenderly offers Charlie Gatorade; they just had a touching father-son moment
jokes.punchline: It's piss — the piss canteen planted at the opening pays off perfectly at the most emotionally intimate moment of the episode
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke and a masterclass in long-game setup/payoff. The piss canteen was planted cold in the first minute of the episode. It pays off at the single most emotionally vulnerable moment — immediately after a touching Frank-Charlie exchange about Frank not being Charlie's real dad. The escalation ('Oh! That's not supposed to be the piss one!' leading to 'That's piss, too!') is perfect. The fact that Frank confused BOTH canteens with piss makes it even better. This is exactly how a great comedy writers' room rewards patient viewers. Structure is essentially perfect.

jokes.text: 'Why is there always a piss one with you?' — escalating to Frank having pissed in BOTH canteens
jokes.setup: Frank's first canteen was piss; he hands Charlie a second
jokes.punchline: 'Oh, I must have got confused and pissed in 'em both.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation of an already-great joke. 'I must have got confused and pissed in 'em both' takes the callback to another level — the safeguard canteen is also piss. Frank's confusion about which canteen he urinated in is both logical (for Frank) and devastating. 'Why is there always a piss one with you?' is a great reactive line. The triple escalation (Gatorade → piss → also piss) is textbook comedy escalation.

jokes.text: Mac drank all the spritzers; Frank offers a spritzer as an alternative to the piss canteens — 'I don't want a fucking spritzer!'
jokes.setup: Frank's alternative to the piss canteens is a wine spritzer
jokes.punchline: Mac drank all the spritzers — the spritzer running gag and the piss running gag collide simultaneously, leaving Charlie with nothing to drink
jokes.explanation: Two running gags collide in perfect comedy convergence. The fact that Mac — who was cut off from spritzers for most of the episode — secretly consumed them all during the emotional moment adds another layer. Charlie's explosive 'I don't want a fucking spritzer!' is cathartic.

jokes.text: The scattered gang reconvenes; Dennis declares 'If there is anything I have learned from this godforsaken rock, it is that I never want to see any of you assholes ever again!'
jokes.setup: Everyone has abandoned the corpse-carrying mission and converged at a pub/shelter
jokes.punchline: Dennis's grand declaration of never wanting to see them again is immediately undercut by the fact they're all together and about to reconcile
jokes.explanation: Standard gang-declaration-of-independence that always leads to them reuniting. Functional but predictable at this point in the series.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Oh, Dee, don't worry about it, because as soon as I figure out who or what I am, you'll never see me again!'
jokes.setup: Mac is also declaring independence; still wrestling with his identity crisis
jokes.punchline: 'As soon as I figure out who or what I am' — the qualifier 'or what' implying he's not sure he's even human, plus this departure is conditional on a process that may never complete
jokes.explanation: Good Mac line. 'Who or what I am' is a funny concession to uncertainty about his fundamental nature. The contingency ('as soon as I figure out') makes the departure threat hollow and self-aware.

jokes.text: The gang gets scolded by an Irish pub patron for speaking too loudly; Dee retorts that she'll speak at whatever volume she wants because 'one volume for every person in the whole wide world — that's socialism'
jokes.setup: An Irish person tells the loud Americans to be quiet
jokes.punchline: Dee invokes 'socialism' as the ideology of enforced quiet — mandatory volume standards as socialist oppression
jokes.explanation: Good political absurdism. The logic — that volume regulation is socialism — is internally coherent nonsense that perfectly captures American political discourse at its most unhinged. 'That's socialism and I won't stand for it' is quotable.

jokes.text: Dee: 'I will speak at whatever volume I choose... if you don't like it, you can suck my big fat dick!'
jokes.setup: Irish patron tells Dee to lower her volume
jokes.punchline: Dee tells him to suck her big fat dick
jokes.explanation: Dee's gendered profanity escalation is characterful. The delivery matters more than the writing here.

jokes.text: 'But you are not in America!' / 'We ARE America, sweetheart! And we carry our country with us wherever we go! Because we love her! And when you love someone, you can't bear to leave 'em behind!'
jokes.setup: Irish patron correctly points out they're not in America
jokes.punchline: The gang's response is an unhinged patriotic speech that secretly doubles as an emotional declaration about carrying the dead body — 'you can't bear to leave 'em behind. Not ever.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent dual-meaning joke. On the surface it's an unhinged American exceptionalism speech. But 'you can't bear to leave 'em behind' is secretly about carrying Charlie's dad — an emotional undercurrent that recontextualizes the absurdism as genuine feeling. The pivot from comedy to earnestness and back is very Always Sunny at its best. Very quotable.

jokes.text: 'One volume? For every single person in the whole wide world? That's socialism, and I won't stand for it!'
jokes.setup: Irish patron asks the gang to speak more quietly
jokes.punchline: Mac interprets a request for quiet as socialist oppression of his right to whatever volume he identifies with
jokes.explanation: Mac's speech is a masterwork of satirical American exceptionalism: volume as identity, quiet as socialism, speaking loudly as freedom. 'We should be able to speak at whatever volume we identify with' perfectly merges his identity arc with political absurdism. Genuinely original and Mac-specific. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Mac mutters 'Get her, banshee' while Dee argues with the Irish patron
jokes.setup: Dee is in a confrontation with an Irish patron
jokes.punchline: Mac quietly encourages the banshee mythology — rooting for Dee in her fight by calling her the banshee
jokes.explanation: Quick callback with great economy. Mac's under-breath 'Get her, banshee' reframes the banshee mythology as a compliment — now her screaming is an asset. Good character beat.

jokes.text: Charlie alone with the body bag on the mountain — collapses in exhaustion and grief
jokes.setup: Everyone has abandoned Charlie; he's left alone to carry the body
jokes.punchline: The comedy of watching Charlie — the least equipped person — be the only one who didn't give up, collapsing under the weight
jokes.explanation: More of a dramatic beat than a joke, but the dark comedy of Charlie's situation — everyone abandoned him with his dead dad — has comedic undertones. Transitions into the emotional monologue.

jokes.text: Charlie's grief monologue: 'You never carried ME up a hill. You never picked me up from school...You didn't bounce me on... You weren't there!'
jokes.setup: Charlie is exhausted and breaks down talking to his dead father's body
jokes.punchline: The parallel between 'carrying the body up the hill' and 'carrying Charlie as a child' — the physical task becomes a metaphor for parental failure, delivered with broken emotional rawness
jokes.explanation: This sits at the comedy-drama line. The humor is dark and uncomfortable — the literal task (carrying a corpse) colliding with emotional truth (Charlie was never 'carried' by his father). 'You didn't bounce me on...' trailing off is both sad and darkly funny in its specificity. It's dark cringe-comedy born of genuine emotion, which is what elevates Always Sunny above pure shock comedy.

jokes.text: 'Ah, Frank's right. I'm glad you're dead. I'm glad you're dead. Now I don't have to spend the rest of my life waiting for you to pick me up.'
jokes.setup: Charlie's grief monologue reaches its emotional climax
jokes.punchline: He inverts the grief — 'I'm glad you're dead' as liberation from waiting for a deadbeat dad who would never come
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark comedy with genuine emotional weight. The turn from grief to 'I'm glad you're dead' is not nihilistic shock — it's psychologically true. Charlie's realization that his dad's death ends the hope-and-disappointment cycle is both heartbreaking and darkly cathartic. 'Now I don't have to spend the rest of my life waiting for you to pick me up' is beautiful writing.

jokes.text: The gang returns in a truck — 'I'm so sorry that I killed your dad! But I'm even more sorry that we left you behind!'
jokes.setup: The gang has had their separate emotional journeys and returned for Charlie
jokes.punchline: Frank's hierarchy of apologies: killing Charlie's dad is bad, but leaving Charlie behind was worse — perfect Frank priorities
jokes.explanation: Good character joke. Frank ranking 'leaving Charlie behind' as more serious than 'giving him COVID' is characteristically Frank — his love for Charlie outranks his responsibility for Shelley's death.

jokes.text: Mac: 'I may be Irish, but I'm American Irish first!'
jokes.setup: The gang is reconciling and deciding to go home
jokes.punchline: Mac has resolved his identity crisis by creating a new hyphenated identity hierarchy — 'American Irish' — which still puts America first
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to Mac's identity arc. The resolution — adding a new layer rather than resolving — is very Mac. 'American Irish first' maintains American exceptionalism while accepting the Irish heritage.

jokes.text: Mac asks how they got the truck — 'The American way. I threw a lot of cash at the owner.'
jokes.setup: Mac wonders how Dennis obtained a truck in rural Ireland
jokes.punchline: 'The American way. I threw a lot of cash at the owner.' — American exceptionalism reduced to 'we pay our way out of everything'
jokes.explanation: Quick clean joke about American imperialism-through-money. Good economy but not exceptional.

jokes.text: They throw Shelley's body off the cliff — it lands with a wet thud on rocks instead of water. 'Oh.' / 'It was supposed to go in the water.' / 'Maybe they usually do this at high tide.'
jokes.setup: The gang finally completes the mission — they chuck Shelley over the cliff
jokes.punchline: The body misses the water and lands on rocks; they rationalize that it was a tidal timing issue
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the whole episode's premise — after all that effort, the burial still goes wrong. The casual rationalization ('maybe they usually do this at high tide') is perfect Always Sunny deflection.

jokes.text: 'Well, the birds will get him.' / 'Yeah, but should we try to scramble our way down there and throw him in the water?' / 'There's a bunch of kids down there.' / 'Oh, that's good, then. They'll find the body.'
jokes.setup: The body has landed on rocks; there are kids below
jokes.punchline: The gang's concern about kids pivots to 'Oh, that's good, then — they'll find the body' as if traumatizing children with a corpse discovery is a helpful outcome
jokes.explanation: Good dark comedy escalation. The gang's instant pivot from 'oh no, kids' to 'great, they'll find the body and call the cops' as a problem-solving measure is characteristically monstrous and logical within their worldview.

jokes.text: 'It'll be sort of like a Stand By Me situation. Yeah. Might be fun for them.'
jokes.setup: Kids are going to find Shelley's mangled body on the rocks
jokes.punchline: Dennis frames the traumatic experience as a Stand By Me movie scenario — which IS a movie about children finding a dead body, suggesting this is a fun adventure for the kids
jokes.explanation: Sharp cultural reference used correctly and darkly. The Stand By Me reference is not just a name-drop — it's precisely the right reference (the whole plot is children discovering a corpse) reframed as a positive outcome for the kids. Dennis treating a traumatic childhood experience as 'fun for them' is perfectly Dennis.

jokes.text: Charlie decides to abandon his dad's burial, dismissing him as 'this dude' — 'Forget this dude. He was a deadbeat, right?'
jokes.setup: Should they try to properly complete the burial?
jokes.punchline: Charlie's emotional journey culminates in 'forget this dude. He was a deadbeat' — full emotional resolution via total dismissal
jokes.explanation: Perfect character payoff. Charlie's emotional arc — from dutiful son carrying a heavy bag to 'forget this dude' — is both funny and emotionally earned. The reduction of his dead father to 'this dude' after the raw grief monologue is excellent dark comedy. 'He was a deadbeat, right?' soliciting agreement from the gang is a funny tag.

jokes.text: 'You want to get some stew?' / 'God, no. That stew's gross.' / [universal agreement] / 'You guys want to go to McDonald's?' / [joyful agreement] 'USA! USA! USA!'
jokes.setup: The gang is heading home; Frank offers the stew from the opening
jokes.punchline: Everyone agrees the stew is gross (the same stew Dennis was eating at the opening), then immediately agrees to McDonald's with patriotic fervor
jokes.explanation: Good closing callback. The gang's unanimous preference for McDonald's over Irish stew as the ultimate American statement lands well. The 'USA' chant as a finale is both funny and thematically appropriate — the whole episode was about Americans being awful abroad.

tmdb_overview: The Gang attempts to ascend a mountain in order for Charlie to fulfill an old and mysterious Irish burial tradition. One by one, the Gang backs out until Charlie is left to honor the dead body alone.
